title: Birds in the sky (90–95)
hookLine: their path is hard to trace, like birds in the air; patient like the earth

lines: A PATH NO ONE CAN TRACE.
cards: A bird lifts off a rooftop, swings out over the street, rides the air for a moment, and it's gone behind the trees. Look back at the sky where it flew. No track, no line, no mark.
A deer leaves footprints in the mud. A boat leaves a wake. A plane leaves a white trail.
A bird leaves the sky exactly as it found it. The Dhammapada uses that empty sky to describe someone whose journey is finished.

teach.b: Chapter seven is about the arahant. The word means the worthy one, the one who deserves honor.
In the Theravada tradition, an arahant is someone who has fully awakened: greed, hatred and delusion gone for good, the journey finished.
Verse ninety says there's no more suffering for one who has finished the journey and thrown off every fetter. Verse ninety-one says the mindful leave home behind like swans leaving a lake.
Then verse ninety-two: they don't hoard, they understand freedom, and “their path is difficult to understand, like that of birds in the air.”
Verse ninety-three says the same of those whose cravings are gone: their path can't be traced either. Why no trace?
Ordinary life leaves a trail of wanting behind it: grudges, cravings, a need to be seen, a need to be right. You can follow a person by those tracks.
An arahant still walks, eats, teaches, helps, but without that trail of clinging. Nothing sticks.
Verse ninety-five gives a second picture: such a person is tolerant like the earth, and clear like a lake without mud. Buddhist traditions hold up different ideals here, and it's fair to say so.
Theravada Buddhists honor the arahant as the goal of the path. Mahayana Buddhists put the bodhisattva at the center, the one who vows to help all beings awaken.
Both honor the qualities in this chapter: tolerance like the earth, and a life that leaves no trail of clinging.

how: In Theravada Buddhism the arahant, one who has fully awakened, is honored as the goal of the path, and the great disciples such as Sariputta and Moggallana are revered as arahants; Mahayana Buddhism centers the bodhisattva ideal.

o: a hermit who lives alone deep in a forest
one fully awakened, with no clinging left
a monk who has served for many decades

games.q: match the pictures in verses ninety to ninety-five.
p: a path no one can trace
tolerant, like the one whose journey is done

s: someone who deserves honor, in whom greed, hatred and delusion have ended.
all Buddhist traditions put the arahant at the center as the ideal
Theravada honors the arahant as the goal; Mahayana centers the bodhisattva.
'no trace' means an arahant stops acting in the world
they still walk, eat, teach and help, but without a trail of clinging.

games.q: you've just done something kind, and nobody noticed. a small voice wants to mention it later. what fits the bird in the sky?
o: let it go; leave no trace.
do it again, louder, so someone sees.
games.why: the bird's path leaves the sky as it found it. the chapter's ideal acts without a trail of wanting to be seen.

practice: If you can see a window, look for a bird and watch the sky close behind it, empty; if not, picture one. Then close your eyes and let each thought be a bird that arrives, crosses the mind and goes.
Let each one pass without drawing a line after it: no follow-up, no commentary, no chase, just open sky and the next bird.

wordCard.voice: Arahant. The worthy one, fully awakened, whose path, like a bird's in the air, leaves no trail of clinging behind.

orig.note: Pali: the worthy one; Sanskrit arhat. Chapter seven is the Arahanta Vagga.

carryVoice: Your line: no trace. The bird leaves the sky as it found it. Day one hundred seventy-six, done.

sources.q: their path is difficult to understand, like that of birds in the air.
